paper_title: Chart-to-Experience Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs for Predicting   Experiential Impact of Charts
caption: The task page for crowdsourced online study
model_annotation: This image displays a crowdsourced online study interface evaluating the experiential impact of a line chart titled “Veterans as share of population,” sourced from the Census Bureau and presented by the Pew Research Center. The chart plots the percentage of veterans in the U.S. population from 1960 to 2010 on a linear scale, with the y-axis ranging from 0% to 15% in increments of 5% and the x-axis spanning decades from 1960 to 2010 at 10-year intervals. A single red solid line with white circular markers shows a generally declining trend: starting at 12.8% in 1960, peaking at 13.8% in 1970, then decreasing to 12.1% in 1980, 11.0% in 1990, 9.4% in 2000, and ending at 7% in 2010. Below the chart, two Likert-scale questions assess user perception: “1. The chart is easily remembered,” with a selected response of “Strongly agree,” and “2. The chart is interesting,” marked as “Insufficient information to answer.” Each question includes a text box for optional justification, limited to 300 characters. A “Chart Scale” slider is visible in the top-right corner, though its current setting is not quantified. The layout suggests a benchmarking task for evaluating how multimodal LLMs predict human experiential responses to data visualizations.

model_annotations.English: This image displays a crowdsourced online study interface for evaluating the experiential impact of a chart, titled “Chart-1,” which plots “Veterans as share of population” over time. The line chart, sourced from the Census Bureau and presented by the Pew Research Center, features a red solid line with circular markers showing a general decline from 12.8% in 1960 to 7% in 2010, with intermediate values labeled at 13.8% (1970), 12.1% (1980), 11.0% (1990), and 9.4% (2000). The x-axis spans years from 1960 to 2010 with 10-year intervals, while the y-axis ranges from 0 to 15% in 5% increments. Below the chart, two Likert-scale questions assess user perception: “1. The chart is easily remembered” is rated “Strongly agree” (blue dot selected on the rightmost option), and “2. The chart is interesting” is marked as “Insufficient information to answer” (checkbox selected). Each question includes a text box prompting users to explain their score, limited to 300 characters. A “Chart Scale” slider appears in the top-right corner, currently set near the left end. The layout suggests a structured human evaluation task for benchmarking multimodal LLMs’ ability to predict chart impact.
